name: Throughput
summary: The volume of data an architecture can process per unit of time — records per second or gigabytes per hour — regardless of any single item's latency.
description: Throughput measures raw processing capacity: how much data moves through the pipeline in a window. It is maximized by batching, wide parallelism across partitions, columnar formats, and vectorized execution that amortize per-record overhead. Throughput often trades against latency — larger batches and buffering raise throughput but delay individual results — so high-throughput designs favor bulk work over fast single-item response.

mechanisms.name: Batching and micro-batching
mechanisms.note: Grouping records amortizes fixed per-operation cost, dramatically raising records processed per second.

mechanisms.name: Partition-level parallelism
mechanisms.note: More partitions mean more independent workers processing in parallel, scaling aggregate throughput.

mechanisms.name: Columnar storage formats
mechanisms.note: Column-oriented files let scans read only needed columns with high compression, cutting IO per row processed.

mechanisms.name: Vectorized query execution
mechanisms.note: Processing batches of values through SIMD-optimized operators moves far more rows per CPU cycle than row-at-a-time.

mechanisms.name: Backpressure handling
mechanisms.note: Flow control lets fast producers and slow consumers coexist without loss, sustaining maximum stable throughput.

manifestations.statement: Large scheduled batches maximize records-per-run by amortizing setup cost, making bulk throughput the whole point of the pattern.
Distributed Spark jobs over columnar Parquet-backed tables sustain very high GB/hr as bronze data is transformed in wide parallel passes.
Partitioned ingest and columnar OLAP storage absorb enormous event volumes per hour, prioritizing bulk ingestion over per-event latency.
Partition parallelism and backpressure let stream operators sustain high steady-state event throughput across a scaled-out cluster.
Fleets emit continuous high-volume telemetry, and partitioned ingest with batched writes keeps aggregate ingestion throughput high.
Columnar Iceberg files scanned in parallel by MPP engines deliver high analytical throughput over one shared copy of the data.
Vectorized single-node execution gives excellent per-core throughput on modest data, but it cannot fan out beyond one machine's limits.
Set-based SQL transformations on MPP warehouses process large tables in bulk, giving high transformation throughput per run.
Pattern-based parallel loads ingest many sources with good throughput, but the many-join read path caps analytical throughput without marts.
Change streams keep steady per-change throughput, but merge/upsert into the target and high-churn tables can throttle sustained volume.
The engine deliberately favors sub-second point queries and small writes over bulk throughput, so heavy backfills strain the serving tier.
Continuous small commits keep tables fresh but produce many small files, trading some bulk throughput and requiring compaction to recover it.
Aggregate throughput is gated by the weakest source and by cross-source data movement, so it rarely matches a co-located warehouse.
Destination SaaS API rate limits cap how many records can be pushed per hour, making downstream throughput the binding constraint.
Bulk embedding of a corpus parallelizes for high indexing throughput, but per-query LLM generation is inherently low-throughput at serving time.
The batch layer maximizes historical reprocessing throughput while the speed layer handles freshness, letting each optimize its own dimension.

tradeoffs.title: Latency
tradeoffs.note: Maximizing throughput favors batching and buffering work for efficiency, which raises per-item and end-to-end latency because records wait to be processed in bulk.

tradeoffs.title: Cost efficiency
tradeoffs.note: Sustaining very high throughput requires large, often always-on clusters sized for peak volume, so aggregate spend rises even as cost per record falls.

tradeoffs.title: Consistency
tradeoffs.note: Pushing volume through heavy parallelism relaxes ordering and exactly-once guarantees, so achieving strict consistency across many concurrent workers caps how much throughput you can extract.
